rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author takes God’s coming as His command amid the visible terrors of resurrection; an appointed term is treated as present, like death that has arrived.
rows.anchor: وأما ﴿ وجاء ربك ﴾ أي أمره فإن المراد به أهوال القيامة المشاهدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first arrival concerns punishment, visible to the eye, while the truth brought in the second phrase is not visible.
rows.anchor: لأن الأول والعذاب وهو مشاهد مرئي بخلاف الحق

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib says itiyān is an easy coming and thus narrower than coming in general; it can describe a questioner walking along his way.
rows.anchor: وقال الراغب الإتيان مجيء بسهولة فهو أخص من مطلق المجيء

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib distinguishes amdad from madd: supplying is usually used for what is welcome, while prolonging is used for what is painful.
rows.anchor: أكثر ما جاء الإمداد في المحبوب نحو ﴿ وأمددناهم بفاكهة ﴾ والمد في المكروه

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib says saqā is for giving drink without effort, while asqā involves effort; asqā is stronger because it provides a source from which to drink.
rows.anchor: فالأول لما لا كلفة فيه ولهذا ذكر في شراب الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAmila usually marks an action extended over time, while faʿala marks quick action; hence sustained good works use the former and prompt action the latter.
rows.anchor: فالأول لما كان من امتداد زمان نحو ﴿ يعملون له ما يشاء ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quʿūd implies remaining, unlike jalūs; the lasting abode is a maqʿad, while a gathering suggests a brief sitting.
rows.anchor: فالأول لما فيه لبث بخلاف الثاني ولهذا يقال قواعد البيت ولا يقال جوالسه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Commentaries are needed because concise wording can hide fine meanings, a writer can omit assumed conditions, and words can bear competing senses or contain errors and omissions.
rows.anchor: وإنما احتيج إلى الشروح لأمور ثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an came in Arabic among eloquent Arabs who knew its apparent wording and rulings; subtle meanings often emerged through inquiry and asking the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وكانوا يعلمون ظواهره وأحكامه أما دقائق باطنه فإنما كان يظهر لهم بعد البحث والنظر

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: When the Companions asked who had never wronged himself, the Prophet explained that the wrong in 6:82 means associating partners with God, citing Luqman 31:13.
rows.anchor: ففسره النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم واستدل عليه بقوله ﴿ إن الشرك لظلم عظيم ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Later Muslims need interpretation even more than the first Arabs, because they lack untrained command of Arabic and cannot independently discern the rulings of surface wording.
rows.anchor: فنحن أشد الناس احتياجا إلى التفسير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tafsir works both by expanding concise expressions and by weighing one possible meaning against another.
rows.anchor: بسط الألفاظ الوجيزة وكشف معانيها وبعضه من قبل ترجيح بعض الاحتمالات على بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laʿalla most commonly expresses expectation or hope for something welcome, and apprehension when the expected matter is unwelcome; al-Tanukhi says it can intensify the latter.
rows.anchor: أشهرها التوقع وهو الترجي في المحبوب نحو ﴿ لعلكم تفلحون ﴾ والإشفاق في المكروه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the command to speak gently to Pharaoh, laʿalla is causal: speak gently so that he may remember or fear.
rows.anchor: الثاني التعليل وخرج عليه ﴿ فقولا له قولا لينا لعله يتذكر أو يخشى ﴾

words: لعل الله يحدث بعد ذلك أمرا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laʿalla can also be interrogative, as shown by its use with verbs meaning know or perceive.
rows.anchor: الثالث الاستفهام وخرج عليه ﴿ لا تدري لعل الله يحدث بعد ذلك أمرا ﴾

rows.speaker: الواقدي
rows.claim: Al-Waqidi, as cited by al-Baghawi, says Qur’anic laʿalla is causal except here, where it means as if; the source calls that simile usage unusual among grammarians.
rows.anchor: وحكى البغوي عن الواقدي أن جميع ما في القرآن من لعل فإنها للتعليل إلا قوله

rows.speaker: البخاري
rows.claim: A report in Sahih al-Bukhari takes laʿalla in this verse as expressing resemblance; another view says it is pure hope relative to the speakers.
rows.anchor: ووقع في صحيح البخاري في قوله ﴿ لعلكم تخلدون ﴾ أن لعل للتشبيه

rows.speaker: أبو مالك
rows.claim: Abu Malik, through al-Suddi, says laʿalla means ‘so that’ throughout the Qur’an except this verse, where it means ‘as if you were immortal.’
rows.anchor: عن أبي مالك قال لعلكم في القرآن بمعنى كي غير آية في الشعراء

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada cites a reading that replaces laʿalla with ka-ann, making the phrase ‘as though you were immortal.’
rows.anchor: قال كان في بعض القراءة / وتتخذون مصانع كأنكم خالدون /

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conjunction aw can express the speaker’s doubt, as when the speakers say they stayed a day or part of a day.
rows.anchor: الشك من المتكلم نحو ﴿ قالوا لبثنا يوما أو بعض يوم ﴾

words: وَإِنَّآ أَوْ إِيَّاكُمْ لَعَلَىٰ هُدًى أَوْ فِى ضَلَٰلٍۢ مُّبِينٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw can leave the matter ambiguous for the listener, as in the deliberately even-handed challenge asking which side is guided and which is plainly astray.
rows.anchor: والإبهام على السامع نحو ﴿ وإنا أو إياكم لعلى هدى أو في ضلال مبين ﴾

words: ففدية من صيام أو صدقة أو نسك
إطعام عشرة مساكين من أوسط ما تطعمون أهليكم أو كسوتهم أو تحرير رقبة
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw marks a choice among alternatives when only one may count as the required expiation or ransom, and permission where the alternatives may be combined.
rows.anchor: والتخيير بين المعطوفين بأن يمتنع الجمع بينهما والإباحة بألا يمتنع الجمع

rows.speaker: ابن هشام
rows.claim: Ibn Hisham answers that the expiation and ransom examples are exclusive only as fulfillment of that one duty; the other acts remain independent good deeds.
rows.anchor: وأجاب ابن هشام بأنه ممتنع بالنسبة إلى وقوع كل كفارة أو فدية بل يقع واحد منهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the clearer choice example of the penalties in 5:33, on the view that the ruler selects one and cannot impose all of them together.
rows.anchor: وأوضح من هذا التمثيل قوله ﴿ أن يقتلوا أو يصلبوا ﴾ الآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw can divide a general report into alternatives said by different groups: some called for Judaism, others Christianity, and different speakers called the messengers sorcerers or madmen.
rows.anchor: والتفصيل بعد الإجمال نحو ﴿ وقالوا كونوا هودا أو نصارى تهتدوا ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw can function like bal, indicating a correction or increase; the source also cites a reading with a still wāw in ‘aw kullamā.’
rows.anchor: والإضراب كبل وخرج عليه ﴿ وأرسلناه إلى مائة ألف أو يزيدون ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw may serve as a plain conjunction equivalent to wāw, joining both possible outcomes rather than setting up an exclusive choice.
rows.anchor: ومطلق الجمع كالواو نحو ﴿ لعله يتذكر أو يخشى ﴾

rows.speaker: الحريري
rows.claim: Al-Hariri and Abu al-Baqaʾ classify aw in ‘or closer’ as approximation; the source records an objection that approximation comes from other wording.
rows.anchor: والتقريب ذكره الحريري وأبو البقاء وجعل منه ﴿ وما أمر الساعة إلا كلمح البصر أو هو أقرب ﴾

words: ما لم تمسوهن أو تفرضوا لهن فريضة
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aw can mean ‘except’ or ‘until,’ with an implicit subjunctive particle; this reading avoids wrongly treating lack of either consummation or a fixed dowry as removing liability for a dowry.
rows.anchor: ومعنى إلا في الاستثناء ومعنى إلى وهاتان ينصب المضارع بعدهما بأن مضمرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expressions of divine amazement are redirected to the audience, since amazement as astonishment implies ignorance and God is exalted above it; the effect is to make people marvel.
rows.anchor: إذا ورد التعجب من الله صرف إلى المخاطب

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sibawayh explains the divine language of hope as telling Moses and Aaron to go with their own hope and expectation that Pharaoh might remember or fear.
rows.anchor: قال سيبويه في قوله تعالى ﴿ لعله يتذكر أو يخشى ﴾ المعنى اذهبا على رجائكما وطمعكما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated woe is not a divine prayer; it means the wrongdoers deserve the phrase Arabs use for people headed for ruin.
rows.anchor: لا نقول هذا دعاء لأن الكلام بذلك قبيح ولكن العرب إنما تكلموا بكلامهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Recitation should be beautified and adorned by a good voice, according to reports cited from Ibn Hibban and others; a beautiful voice increases the Qur’an’s beauty.
rows.anchor: يسن تحسين الصوت بالقراءة وتزيينها لحديث ابن حبان وغيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those without a naturally beautiful voice should improve it as much as they can, without excessive stretching that distorts recitation.
rows.anchor: فإن لم يكن حسن الصوت حسنه ما استطاع بحيث لا يخرج إلى حد التمطيط

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi’s Mukhtasar says there is no objection to reciting with melodies; a report from al-Rabiʿ al-Jizi says he disliked it.
rows.anchor: وأما القراءة بالألحان فنص الشافعي في المختصر أنه لا بأس بها

rows.speaker: الرافعي
rows.claim: Al-Rafiʿi says the jurists do not really differ: dislike applies to excessive elongation, overfilled vowels, or assimilation where it does not belong.
rows.anchor: قال الرافعي قال الجمهور ليست على قولين بل المكروه أن يفرط في المد

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: Al-Nawawi’s Rawda says this excess is forbidden and makes the reader sinful, with the listener also sinful; he takes this to be what al-Shafiʿi meant by dislike.
rows.anchor: والصحيح أن الإفراط على الوجه المذكور حرام يفسق به القارئ ويأثم المستمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report attributed to al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi commands recitation in Arab melodies and warns against the styles of scriptural communities and immoral people, likening later recitation to song and monastic chanting.
rows.anchor: اقرؤوا القرآن بلحون العرب وأصواتها وإياكم ولحون أهل الكتابين وأهل الفسق

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: Al-Nawawi recommends asking a good-voiced reader to recite and listening to that recitation, based on a sound hadith.
rows.anchor: ويستحب طلب القراءة من حسن الصوت والأصغاء إليها للحديث الصحيح

rows.speaker: النووي
rows.claim: Al-Nawawi permits group recitation and turns, where one person reads a portion and the next continues with another portion.
rows.anchor: ولا بأس باجتماع الجماعة في القراءة ولا بإدارتها

words: فِىٓ أَىِّ صُورَةٍۢ مَّا شَآءَ رَكَّبَكَ
rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A weak-chain report says the Prophet corrected a father who guessed whether a child would resemble either parent: after the sperm settles, God establishes the lineages reaching back to Adam; he glossed ‘in whatever form He willed’ as ‘He shaped you.’
rows.anchor: بسند ضعيف من طريق موسى بن علي بن رباح عن أبيه عن جده أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Umar reports the Prophet as saying that the righteous are so named because they were good to their parents and children.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عمر عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم قال ( إنما سماهم الأبرار لأنهم بروا الآباء والأبناء )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A singular may be addressed in dual form: ‘cast both of you’ is variously addressed to Hell’s keeper Malik, the keepers or guards collectively, or literally the two angels assigned to each person.
rows.anchor: خطاب الواحد بلفظ الإثنين نحو ﴿ ألقيا في جهنم ﴾ والخطاب لمالك خازن النار

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi classifies ‘your supplication has been answered’ as singular address to Moses, because he alone made the supplication; alternatively it addresses both since Aaron’s amen made him one of the supplicants.
rows.anchor: وجعل المهدوي من هذا النوع ﴿ قال قد أجيبت دعوتكما ﴾ قال الخطاب لموسى وحده

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says Pharaoh addresses two people with a singular vocative, singling out Moses because of their special relation through his upbringing.
rows.anchor: أحدهما أنه أفرده بالنداء لإدلاله عليه بالتربية

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya’s other explanation is that Moses alone is named because he bears the mission and signs, while Aaron follows him.
rows.anchor: والآخر لأنه صاحب الرسالة والآيات وهارون تبع له ذكره ابن عطية

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari adds that Pharaoh avoided addressing Aaron because Aaron was more eloquent than Moses and Pharaoh feared his tongue.
rows.anchor: وذكر في الكشاف آخر وهو أن هارون لما كان أفصح من موسى نكب فرعون عن خطابه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya explains the singular ‘you will suffer’ as directed to Adam because he was addressed first and was the main subject.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية أفرده بالشقاء لأنه المخاطب أولا والمقصود في الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation is that hardship in worldly livelihood was assigned to men.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأنه الله جعل الشقاء في معيشة الدنيا في جانب الرجال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation is polite omission of the woman, in keeping with the saying that good manners conceal women.
rows.anchor: وقيل إغضاء عن ذكر المرأة كما قيل من الكرم ستر الحرم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address to Moses and Aaron uses plural morphology for two addressees.
rows.anchor: خطاب الإثنين لفظ الجمع كقوله ﴿ أن تبوآ لقومكما بمصر بيوتا واجعلوا بيوتكم قبلة ﴾

words: وما تتلو منه من قرآن ولا تعملون من عمل
rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari says the speech shifts from the Prophet alone to a plural verb to include the whole community with him in the act.
rows.anchor: قال ابن الأنباري جمع في الفعل الثالث ليدل على أن الأمة داخلون مع النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The converse pattern also occurs: plural address followed by a singular form.
rows.anchor: العشرون عكسه نحو ﴿ وأقيموا الصلاة ﴾ ﴿ وبشر المؤمنين ﴾

words: أجئتنا لتلفتنا عما وجدنا عليه آباءنا وتكون لكما الكبرياء في الأرض
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another address pattern begins with one addressee and then turns to two.
rows.anchor: الحادي والعشرون خطاب الإثنين بعد الواحد نحو ﴿ أجئتنا لتلفتنا عما وجدنا عليه آباءنا وتكون لكما الكبرياء في الأرض ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The inverse address pattern also appears: a dual audience receives a singular form, as when Pharaoh asks Moses, ‘Who is your Lord?’ while addressing both brothers.
rows.anchor: الثاني والعشرون عكسه نحو ﴿ فمن ربكما يا موسى ﴾

words: فَإِن كُنتَ فِى شَكٍّ مِّمَّآ أَنزَلْنَآ إِلَيْكَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A direct address may name one person while intending someone else: commands to the Prophet can target his community, and the hypothetical doubt in 10:94 is an allusion to disbelievers.
rows.anchor: الخطاب له والمراد أمته لأنه صلى الله عليه وسلم كان تقيا وحاشاه من طاعة الكفار

words: فَإِن كُنتَ فِى شَكٍّ مِّمَّآ أَنزَلْنَآ إِلَيْكَ
rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says the Prophet neither doubted nor asked; the conditional address is not a report of his actual state.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس في هذه الآية قال لم يشك صلى الله عليه وسلم ولم يسأل

words: واسأل من أرسلنا من قبلك من رسلنا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source places other commands such as ‘ask those We sent before you’ and ‘do not be among the ignorant’ in this same indirect-address pattern.
rows.anchor: ومثله ﴿ واسأل من أرسلنا من قبلك من رسلنا ﴾ الآية ﴿ فلا تكونن من الجاهلين ﴾

words: لقد أنزلنا إليكم كتابا فيه ذكركم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reverse pattern addresses someone else in form while intending the particular person meant by the words.
rows.anchor: الرابع والعشرون خطاب الغير والمراد به العين نحو ﴿ لقد أنزلنا إليكم كتابا فيه ذكركم ﴾

words: ألم تر أن الله يسجد له
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some خطاب is general rather than aimed at one listener; its scene is so evident that anyone capable of seeing is included in the address.
rows.anchor: لم يقصد بذلك خطاب معين بل كل أحد وأخرج في صورة الخطاب لقصد العموم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In one example, the opening addresses the Prophet and the following command shifts to the disbelievers, as confirmed by the next question asking whether they will submit.
rows.anchor: خوطب به النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ثم قال للكفار ﴿ فاعلموا أنما أنزل بعلم الله ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source also cites the shift in ‘We sent you as a witness … that you may believe,’ for readers who pronounce the final verb with second-person plural tāʾ.
rows.anchor: ومنه ﴿ إنا أرسلناك شاهدا ﴾ إلى قوله ﴿ لتؤمنوا ﴾ فيمن قرأ بالفوقية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: خطاب al-talwīn is another name for iltifāt, the change in grammatical person or address.
rows.anchor: السابع والعشرون خطاب التلوين وهو الإلتفات

words: فَقَالَ لَهَا وَلِلْأَرْضِ ٱئْتِيَا طَوْعًا أَوْ كَرْهًا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an can address inanimate things in the form used for rational beings, as in the command to heaven and earth.
rows.anchor: خطاب الجمادات خطاب من يعقل نحو ﴿ فقال لها وللأرض ائتيا طوعا أو كرها ﴾

words: وعلى الله فتوكلوا إن كنتم مؤمنين
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An address can be framed to spur its audience on, as in the challenge to trust in God if they are believers.
rows.anchor: التاسع والعشرون خطاب التهييج نحو ﴿ وعلى الله فتوكلوا إن كنتم مؤمنين ﴾

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Jundab ibn ʿAbd Allah reports the Prophet saying to kill a sorcerer if found; the Prophet recited this verse and explained it as meaning the sorcerer does not succeed wherever found.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم ( إذا وجدتم الساحر فاقتلوه ) ثم قرأ

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports a good-chain Prophetic explanation that the constricted life mentioned in the verse means the punishment of the grave.
rows.anchor: وأخرج البزار بسند جيد عن أبي هريرة عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم ﴿ فإن له معيشة ضنكا ﴾ قال ( عذاب القبر )

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: A report stopped at Ibn Masʿud says every Qur’anic letter has a boundary and every boundary an opening or point of access.
rows.anchor: عن ابن مسعود موقوفا ( إن هذا القرآن ليس منه حرف إلا له حد ولكل حد مطلع )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation of the Qur’an’s outer and inner aspects is that probing its inner sense and comparing it with its wording reveals its meaning.
rows.anchor: أنك إذا بحثت عن باطنها وقسته على ظاهرها وقفت على معناها

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Another report says each verse has already been acted on by some people and will be acted on by others later.
rows.anchor: أن ما من آية إلا عمل بها قوم ولها قوم سيعملون بها كما قال ابن مسعود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further explanation identifies the outer aspect with the wording and the inner aspect with its interpretation.
rows.anchor: ظاهرها لفظها وباطنها تأويلها

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayd considers this explanation most sound: historical stories outwardly report earlier peoples’ destruction, while inwardly warning later generations not to repeat their deeds.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عبيد وهو أشبهها بالصواب إن القصص التي قصها الله تعالى عن الأمم الماضية

rows.speaker: ابن النقيب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Naqib says the outer sense is what scholars of exoteric learning understand, while the inner sense contains secrets God disclosed to people of spiritual realization.
rows.anchor: إن ظهرها ما ظهر من معانيها لأهل العلم بالظاهر وبطنها ما تضمنته من الأسرار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The boundary of a passage is the limit of the meaning God intends; another view makes it the measure of reward or punishment due for a ruling.
rows.anchor: ومعنى قوله ( ولكل حرف حد ) أي منتهى فيما أراد الله من معناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An opening is a route to understanding an obscure meaning or ruling; alternatively, it is where its deserved reward or punishment is disclosed in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: لكل غامض من المعاني والأحكام مطلع يتوصل به إلى معرفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another formulation calls the outer aspect recitation, the inner aspect understanding, the boundary the rulings of lawful and unlawful acts, and the opening insight into promise and warning.
rows.anchor: الظاهر التلاوة والباطن الفهم والحد أحكام الحلال والحرام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak reports Ibn ʿAbbas saying the Qur’an has many branches, outer and inner dimensions, and inexhaustible wonders; its outer aspect is recitation and inner aspect interpretation, so one should study with scholars and avoid fools.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس قال إن القرآن ذو شجون وفنون وظهور وبطون لا تنقضي عجائبه

rows.speaker: أبو الدرداء
rows.claim: Ibn Sabʿ cites Abu al-Dardaʾ: a person has not fully understood until he recognizes multiple facets in the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: ورد عن أبي الدرداء أنه قال لا يفقه الرجل كل الفقه حتى يجعل للقرآن وجوها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Order can follow revelation chronology, as in naming the scriptures of Abraham and Moses or placing Torah and Gospel before the Criterion.
rows.anchor: أو باعتبار الإنزال كقوله ﴿ صحف إبراهيم وموسى ﴾

words: إن الصفا والمروة من شعائر الله
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Order may follow duty and prescribed sequence; the Prophet accordingly said to begin with what God began with, regarding Safa and Marwa.
rows.anchor: أو باعتبار الوجوب والتكليف نحو ﴿ اركعوا واسجدوا ﴾

words: ما يكون من نجوى ثلاثة إلا هو رابعهم ولا خمسة إلا هو سادسهم
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordering may reflect inherent numerical order; ‘two and singly’ is instead arranged to urge people to gather for good.
rows.anchor: وأما قوله ﴿ أن تقوموا لله مثنى وفرادى ﴾ فللحث على الجماعة والاجتماع على الخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Causal sequence can explain divine names: might precedes judgment because power enables rule, and knowledge precedes precision; in the legal context of al-Anʿam, wisdom precedes knowledge.
rows.anchor: السابع السببية كتقديم العزيز على الحكيم لأنه عز فحكم والعليم عليه لأن الإحكام والإتقان ناشئ عن العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sequence can mark causation: worship brings aid, repentance brings purification, slander causes sin, and the gaze can lead to sexual desire.
rows.anchor: ومنه تقديم العبادة على الاستعانة في سورة الفاتحة لأنها سبب حصول الإعانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Order may reflect relative frequency: disbelievers, wrongdoers, male thieves, and female adulterers are named first because the author says each is more common in that group.
rows.anchor: الثامن الكثرة كقوله ﴿ فمنكم كافر ومنكم مؤمن ﴾ لأن الكفار أكثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mercy is usually placed before punishment in the Qur’an, matching the report that God’s mercy has prevailed over His anger.
rows.anchor: ومنه تقديم الرحمة على العذاب حيث وقع في القرآن غالبا ولهذا ورد ( إن رحمتي غلبت غضبي )

words: إن من أزواجكم وأولادكم عدوا لكم
rows.speaker: ابن الحاجب
rows.claim: Ibn al-Hajib says spouses precede children because spouses are more often enemies; wealth precedes children because it is more consistently a source of temptation and can lead a person to transgress.
rows.anchor: إنما قدم الأزواج لأن المقصود الإخبار أن فيهم أعداء ووقوع ذلك في الأزواج أكثر منه في الأولاد

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisaʾi says waykaʾanna conveys regret and astonishment, originating in waylaka, with the kāf as a genitive pronoun.
rows.anchor: قال الكسائي كلمة تندم وتعجب وأصله ويلك والكاف ضمير مجرور

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash parses way as an exclamation meaning ‘I wonder,’ kāf as a vocative particle, and anna with an omitted lām, yielding ‘I wonder that God…’
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش وي اسم فعل بمعنى أعجب والكاف حرف خطاب وأن على إضمار اللام

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalil treats way as a word on its own and kaʾanna as a separate particle of emphasis rather than comparison.
rows.anchor: وقال الخليل وي وحدها وكأن كلمة مستقلة للتحقيق لا للتشبيه

rows.speaker: ابن الأنباري
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbari offers three parses: wayk plus anna meaning ‘do you not see,’ way laka meaning ‘woe to you,’ or way of wonder plus kaʾanna, joined in writing through frequent use.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن الأنباري يحتمل وي كأنه ثلاثة أوجه أن يكون ويك حرفا وأنه حرف والمعنى ألم تر

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas, through al-Kalbi and Abu Salih, interprets the letters kaf-ha-ya-ʿayn-sad as the All-sufficient, Guide, Knower, and Truthful.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس في قوله ﴿ كهيعص ﴾ قال الكاف الكافي والهاء الهادي والعين العالم

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: A report through al-Kalbi, Abu Salih, and Umm Haniʾ attributes to the Prophet the expansions ‘Sufficient, Guide, Trustworthy, Knowing, Truthful.’
rows.anchor: عن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال كاف هاد أمين عالم صادق

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: ʿIkrima interprets these letters as ‘I am the Great, Guide, Exalted, Trustworthy, Truthful.’
rows.anchor: وأخرج ابن أبي حاتم عن عكرمة في قوله ﴿ كهيعص ﴾ قال يقول أنا الكبير الهادي علي أمين صادق

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb says ṭā in Ṭā Hā and Ṭā Sīn Mīm comes from dhu al-tawl; in the latter, sīn is from al-Quddus and mīm from al-Rahman.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عن محمد بن كعب في قوله ﴿ طه ﴾ قال الطاء من ﴿ ذي الطول ﴾

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn Jubayr says the letters ḥāʾ and mīm in Ḥā Mīm derive from al-Rahman and al-Rahim.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عن سعيد بن جبير في قوله ﴿ حم ﴾ قال حاء اشتقت من الرحمن وميم اشتقت من الرحيم

rows.speaker: محمد بن كعب
rows.claim: Muhammad ibn Kaʿb derives ḥāʾ and mīm from al-Rahman, ʿayn from al-ʿAlim, sīn from al-Quddus, and qāf from al-Qahir.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عن محمد بن كعب في قوله ﴿ حم عسق ﴾ قال الحاء والميم من الرحمن والعين من العليم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says the openings of all surahs are spelled-out, detached letters.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عن مجاهد قال فواتح السور كلها هجاء مقطع

rows.speaker: سالم بن عبد الله
rows.claim: Salim ibn ʿAbd Allah says alif-lam-mim, ḥā-mīm, nūn, and similar openings are divine names split into letters.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عن سالم بن عبد الله قال ﴿ الم ﴾ و ﴿ حم ﴾ و ﴿ ن ﴾ ونحوها اسم الله مقطعة

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says the surah openings are names of the Lord distributed through the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: وأخرج عن السدي قال فواتح السور أسماء من أسماء الرب جل جلاله فرقت في القرآن

rows.speaker: الكرماني
rows.claim: Al-Kirmani says qaf is a letter taken from the divine names Qadir and Qahir.
rows.anchor: وحكى الكرماني في قوله ﴿ ق ﴾ إنه حرف من اسمه قادر وقاهر

rows.speaker: غيره
rows.claim: Another scholar says nun is a key to the divine names Nur and Nasir.
rows.anchor: وحكى غيره في قوله ﴿ ن ﴾ إنه مفتاح اسمه تعالى نور وناصر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author reduces these views to one account: detached letters, each taken from one divine name; Arabic also allows a word to be represented by only part of it, as the cited poems illustrate.
rows.anchor: كل حرف منها مأخوذ من اسم من أسمائه تعالى والاكتفاء ببعض الكلمة معهود في العربية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry demonstrates Arabic clipping: qaf can stand for waqaftu, fa for fa-sharr, ta for tashāʾ, and another line likewise omits part of a word.
rows.anchor: قال الشاعر ( قلت لها قفي فقالت قاف ) أي وقفت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinas al-mudariʿ type differs by a neighboring letter, whether at the beginning, middle, or end; the source illustrates it with yanhawna/yanʾawna.
rows.anchor: ومنها المضارع وهو أن يختلفا بحرف مقارب في المخرج سواء كان في الأول أو الوسط أو الآخر

words: تَفْرَحُونَ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ بِغَيْرِ ٱلْحَقِّ وَبِمَا كُنتُمْ تَمْرَحُونَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinas al-lahiq type differs by a non-neighboring letter; examples include hamaza/lamaza, shahid/shadid, tafraḥun/tamraḥun, and amr/al-amn.
rows.anchor: ومنها اللاحق بأن يختلفا بحرف غير مقارب فيه كذلك كقوله ﴿ ويل لكل همزة لمزة ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The compound type of jinas combines a whole word with part of another, as in juruf hār/fanhar.
rows.anchor: ومنها المرفق وهو ما تركب من كلمة وبعض أخرى كقوله ﴿ جرف هار فانهار ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The written or graphic type differs through letters resembling one another in form, such as ḍād and ẓāʾ in nāḍira/nāẓira.
rows.anchor: ومنها اللفظي بأن يختلفا بحرف مناسب للآخر مناسبة لفظية كالضاد والظاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinas al-qalb reverses the order of letters, illustrated by farraqt between the Children of Israel.
rows.anchor: ومنها تجنيس القلب بأن يختلفا في ترتيب الحروف نحو ﴿ فرقت بين بني إسرائيل ﴾

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Derivational jinas brings together words sharing a root, illustrated by rawh/rayhan, aqim/qayyim, and wajjahtu/wajhi.
rows.anchor: ومنها تجنيس الإشتقاق بأن يجتمعا في أصل الإشتقاق ويسمى المقتضب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jinas al-itlaq joins words only by resemblance, with examples including janna/jannatayn, ʿamali/ al-qalin, yuwari, irtad, and the repeated ard and duʿaʾ forms.
rows.anchor: ومنها تجنيس الإطلاق بأن يجتمعا في المشابهة فقط كقوله ﴿ وجنى الجنتين ﴾
